first.rationale: The two symptoms that are actually degrading (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are causally linked, and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a single slot spent there plausibly moves both. Promotional pricing is the tempting answer to the competitor's entry pricing, but memory_73 explicitly records a retention penalty and an explicit warning against generalizing it; under a 'sustainable long-term qualified revenue' objective that is disqualifying, not merely cautionary. Referral incentives (memory_57) target established customers and do not touch the failing funnel stage; enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) is sound but addresses a segment that is not where the regression is. Activation messaging (memory_91) is the strongest alternative and I would run it next; I rank it second only because it treats the downstream symptom while the upstream leak persists. I am spending both verification pulls on memory_31 and memory_86 because they are the load-bearing evidence for my chosen action and I suspect they may not be independent \u2014 'cutting required fields at signup' and 'shortening onboarding' could be two consolidations of the same underlying experiment, which would mean I have one data point rather than two corroborating ones. If the archive shows a shared source, distinct effect sizes, or that the original lift was measured on a cohort unlike today's competitor-pressured SMB inflow, I will downscale to a guarded test or switch to activation_messaging. Downstream risk I am explicitly flagging: stripping signup fields can degrade qualification data and misroute enterprise prospects away from the demo-request path that memory_44 shows outperforms self-serve on pipeline quality \u2014 i.e. a real risk of buying activation lift with qualified-revenue loss. I will therefore gate the test to self-serve SMB traffic, preserve enterprise routing signals, and instrument pipeline quality and 30-day retention as guardrail metrics, not just completion rate. All inherited findings are 15-64 days old and predate the competitor's entry; I am treating them as informative priors, not settled facts.

mid.rationale: Verification resolved my main worry: exp_31 and exp_86 are distinct experiments, not two consolidations of one source, so I have genuine corroboration rather than a single data point counted twice. Both are marked confirmed. exp_86 is the stronger warrant for this cycle \u2014 completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and retention +3%, meaning the onboarding-shortening lever improved rather than traded away durability, which is exactly what a sustainable-qualified-revenue objective wants. exp_31 also holds but is weaker on the metric I actually care about: signup +15% and activation +9% converted to only +4% qualified revenue with retention -1%, i.e. much of the top-of-funnel lift did not survive to qualified revenue. So I am weighting the flow-shortening component over aggressive signup-field stripping. One explicit scope limit from the archive: exp_31 was confirmed on SMB and NOT replicated on other segments. I am therefore gating the test to self-serve SMB and not extrapolating to enterprise. This also protects the memory_44 finding \u2014 enterprise converts better through the sales-assisted demo-request path, and I will preserve enterprise routing signals rather than let field-stripping misroute high-value prospects into self-serve. That remains my live downstream risk: buying activation lift at the cost of qualification data and pipeline quality. I hold promotional_pricing rejected despite the competitor's entry pricing; memory_73 records a material 30-day retention hit and an explicit warning against generalizing it, and matching a price attack with a lever known to erode durable revenue is the wrong trade under this objective. Residual uncertainty I am not pretending away: all inherited results predate the competitor launch, so today's SMB inflow may be more price-motivated and less responsive to friction reduction than the original cohorts; and the -6%/-4% declines could share an unmeasured cause that onboarding changes will not touch. Guardrails, not just completion rate: 30-day retention, qualified revenue per cohort, and enterprise pipeline quality, with a pre-committed stop if retention or pipeline quality degrades. activation_messaging (memory_91) is my ranked-second option and the natural next slot if this reads flat.

final2.rationale: The competitor's second cut is real news and it raises urgency, but urgency is not evidence. Nothing arrived today that changes what promotional_pricing is known to do. memory_73 records it as an acquisition lever \u2014 strong acquisition and revenue lift in price-sensitive SMB \u2014 that materially reduced 30-day retention, with an explicit warning against generalizing it. Leadership's implied ask is to use it as a retention shield for accounts already in churn conversations, and that is an off-label extrapolation: the archived support is for winning new price-sensitive signups, not for holding existing ones. Deploying it here would spend my only slot on the one lever whose documented failure mode is precisely the metric under attack, and it would anchor a price war against a competitor who has already shown willingness to cut twice and can presumably cut again. That is a losing position to enter on a same-day decision. I am holding simplify_onboarding, primarily the exp_86 flow-shortening component: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, retention +3%. That retention sign matters more now than it did on day 76 \u2014 faster time-to-value is a durable defense against price-based churn, because accounts that have reached a first meaningful outcome are harder to buy away than accounts still stuck in setup. It is the slower response, and I am honest that it will not stop this week's churn conversations. Scope limits I am keeping: gate to self-serve SMB, since exp_31 was confirmed on SMB and explicitly not replicated elsewhere; preserve enterprise demo-request routing per memory_44 so field-stripping does not misroute high-value prospects into self-serve. Guardrails remain 30-day retention, qualified revenue per cohort, and enterprise pipeline quality, with a pre-committed stop. What I genuinely do not know: whether the churning accounts are recoverable by any product lever on this timescale, and whether the -6%/-4% declines share an unmeasured cause upstream of onboarding. Both inherited results predate the competitor entirely, so today's SMB inflow may be more price-motivated than the original cohorts. The right home for the pricing question is a scoped commercial decision with real margin and win-back analysis \u2014 not this week's single experiment slot, and not a same-day call made under churn pressure. If leadership wants pricing action anyway, it should be a narrow defensive retention offer to identified at-risk accounts with retention instrumented as the primary metric, run as a separate decision, not as a broad promotional rollout justified by memory_73. activation_messaging (memory_91) remains my ranked-second slot next cycle.
